title: LoadGen repeatability and warmup best practices for throughput experiments
content:
Purpose and scope:

This document collects operational guidance and concrete configuration recommendations for running reliable and repeatable throughput experiments against the serving runtime. It focuses on three pain points we repeatedly observe: noisy warmup behavior, non-deterministic batching and caching effects, and measurement drift across repeated runs. The goal is to provide a concise lab playbook that engineers can follow to produce comparable, debuggable throughput numbers and to accelerate root-cause profiling of bottlenecks.

Audience:
- Performance engineers and SREs running load campaigns
- Runtime developers validating kernel changes
- Solutions engineers reproducing customer performance reports

High-level summary of recommended approach:
1) Use a deterministic, instrumented load generator with fixed seeds where sampling is involved.
2) Isolate state across runs: process restarts, clean KV caches, and ephemeral model worker pools.
3) Adopt a two-phase run: warmup (to stabilize JIT/compilation/kernels and caches) followed by measurement windows.
4) Repeat each experiment N times (N >= 3, N recommended = 5) and report median plus IQR; if variance > 10% investigate.
5) Capture system-level telemetry (GPU SM utilization, PCIe, host CPU steal, network queues) synchronously with loadgen traces.

Load generator configuration recommendations (practical defaults):
- generator: redwood-loadgen (see linked github) or k6 with custom HTTP client.
- seed: set random seed explicitly (e.g., --seed=42) to ensure synthetic prompt selection repeatability.
- concurrency mode: prefer 'steady concurrency' over 'open-loop QPS' for throughput tests where worker utilization matters. For latency-sensitive SLOs use closed-loop to avoid unbounded queue growth.
- concurrency value: pick a range that spans under-utilized to saturated. For example, for a 4x A100 pool: [4, 8, 16, 32, 64].
- request shape: provide distribution file with percentile token lengths (p50/p90/p99). Use the same file for all runs. Example: --prompt-dist=dist_32_128_512.json.
- batch hints: when testing compiler/runtime batching strategies, pass explicit target batch sizes and disable autoscaling (e.g. --target-batch=32 --disable-autoscale).
- run duration: warmup: 6 minutes; measurement: 10 minutes. Shorter runs (<5m) are noisy; longer runs (>30m) increase CI cost.
- ramp: linear ramp over 30s at start of warmup to avoid initial thundering herd.
- jitter: minimize synthetic inter-request jitter during throughput runs; set jitter=0 for repeatability tests.

Warmup strategy rationale and steps:
- Why warmup is necessary: model runtimes compile kernels, lazy-load weights, build KV caches, and the serving runtime adapts batching parameters. These transient behaviors skew initial samples.
- Warmup phase: allocate a dedicated warmup window in which the load generator exercises the full distribution of request sizes and features. Run warmup long enough to see stabilization in endpoint-level latency and GPU utilization (visual rule: 2 successive 60s windows with <3% change in mean latency and GPU SM%).
- Warmup tokens vs time: prefer timed warmups (minutes) since token-based warmups vary with prompt size. Example: warmup_time=6m.
- Pre-warm alternatives: pre-loading models and pre-creating workers via an orchestration script can reduce time but should be documented and consistent across experiments.
- Post-warm flush: after warmup, allow a 15s settling period to let in-flight KV writes flush. Then begin measurement window.

State isolation and reproducibility checklist (run before every trial):
- Restart model worker processes (or rollout a new revision) to clear any internal allocator state.
- Clear KV/prefix caches in the runtime: run admin API /internal/clear-cache or restart service.
- Ensure no other workloads on GPUs: confirm via nvidia-smi and disable background batch jobs.
- Confirm model binary and quantization profile are pinned; use SHA or exact artifact tag.
- Record environment variables that affect run (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL, OMP_NUM_THREADS).
- Capture exact loadgen commandline and seed.

Measurement windows, metrics to collect, and aggregation rules:
- Primary metrics: overall throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec), p50/p90/p99 latency (server-side, end-to-end), GPU SM% utilization, GPU memory headroom, host cpu load, system PCIe utilization.
- Secondary metrics: queue length, batch size distribution, KV cache hit ratio, RPC retry counts, gRPC channel saturation.
- Measurement granularity: collect 1s granularity counters for the entire run and aggregate over the measurement window after warmup.
- Aggregation rules: discard first X seconds as warmup trim (e.g., first 30s of measurement window), compute median throughput across per-second samples, and report 25th/75th percentile for variability. If per-second throughput CV > 8%, flag run as unstable.
- Repeats: run the full warmup+measurement sequence 5 times back-to-back. Between trials, perform the state isolation checklist.

Handling non-determinism and common sources of noise:
- JIT/compilation: always include at least one long warmup run after any binary/kernel change. For CI, mark new kernel changes as 'noisy' until two clean runs are observed.
- Background OS activity: pin processes to cores and isolate NIC interrupts where possible (irqbalance tweaks). Document kernel version and NUMA config.
- Network jitter: run load generators locally in the same network region or on the same rack to minimize variability. Use loopback tests to validate service alone.
- Autoscaling and eviction: disable or freeze autoscalers during bench runs. Record any eviction/placement events from orchestration logs.
- Memory pressure and GC: for runtimes with GC, ensure Java/Python heaps are configured so that GC cycles are idle during measurement windows or are recorded and excluded if they occur.

Profiling and diagnosing regressions during throughput campaigns:
- Correlate per-second throughput dips with system traces (dstat, nvidia-smi, perf records).
- Capture a short flamegraph from a representative worker during a dip: run 30s perf record with symbolized output.
- Use batch-size distribution logs to see if runtime suddenly chose smaller batches due to request timing; if so inspect request arrival variance.
- If GPU utilization drops while latency and queue lengths grow, suspect PCIe contention or interconnect issues.

Recommended experiments (examples):
1) Baseline: single model version, pinned hardware, range of concurrency values, 5 repeats per point.
2) Kernel change A/B: deploy new kernel on a subset of workers and run canary trials with identical loadgen seed to isolate behavioral differences.
3) Batch-policy sweep: test '--target-batch' values [1,8,16,32,64] with autoscaling off to see throughput vs latency tradeoffs.
4) Cache-hit sensitivity: run with KV cache disabled vs enabled and quantify delta on token/sec and p99 latency.

Quickstart script (example):
- prepare: ./scripts/bench/setup_env.sh --model=my-model:sha1 --gpu-pool=4xA100
- warmup+measure (one trial): ./bin/redwood-loadgen --seed=42 --concurrency=32 --prompt-dist=dist_32_128_512.json --warmup=6m --measure=10m --jitter=0 --output=run-32.json
- post-run: ./scripts/bench/collect-metrics.py --run=run-32.json --out=summary-32.csv
- repeat trial: ./scripts/bench/reset_state.sh && sleep 10 && (rerun loadgen)

Report template for every experiment (minimum):
- run_id, model_tag, hardware_pool, loadgen_cmdline, seed, warmup_time, measure_time, repeats, per-point median throughput, IQR, p90/p99 latency, notes on anomalies.

Common pitfalls and debugging tips (short):
- Pitfall: inconsistent prompt distribution between runs. Tip: commit a distribution file to the bench artifact directory and reference by SHA.
- Pitfall: forgetting to pin model binary leading to bitrot. Tip: always use artifact tag + checksum in run metadata.
- Pitfall: measuring from a distant region. Tip: co-locate loadgens and collectors.

Next steps and outstanding questions:
- Automate state isolation in CI to reduce human error (JIRA-ENG-4921).
- Add a small 'golden' workload with deterministic prompts for quick health checks.
- Investigate faster kernel warmup paths so warmup window can be reduced cost-effectively.

Appendix: useful commands
- Restart worker pool: ./infra/ctl restart-pool --pool serving-a100-4
- Clear runtime cache: curl -XPOST http://localhost:8080/internal/clear-cache
- Collect GPU telemetry: nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o TD > gpu-dmon.csv

End of document.
